title: Ὀδυσσεὺς Τηλεμάχῳ φαίνεται
about: Telemachus answers the questions Odysseus put to him at the end of the last part. The land is not hostile to him, and he has no brothers to blame: Arcesius had one son, Laertes, and Laertes one son, Odysseus, and Odysseus only himself. So the suitors from all the islands crowd his house and eat it away, while his mother can neither refuse them nor bring it to an end. He sends Eumaeus to tell Penelope that he is safe. Eumaeus asks whether he should take the news to the grieving Laertes as well, and Telemachus tells him to have the housekeeper sent to the old man in secret instead. As the swineherd sets off, Athena comes to the door of the hut, unseen by Telemachus and seen only by Odysseus and the dogs. She tells Odysseus to speak out to his son, touches him with her golden wand, and gives him back a young man’s body and clothes. Telemachus, afraid that a god is before him, begs to be spared. Odysseus says that he is his father, and Telemachus, still unconvinced, says that some power must be enchanting him; Odysseus answers that Athena makes him now a beggar and now a young man.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: A reply formula. τόν ‘him’ is a pronoun, not the article, and means Odysseus; αὖ is ‘in turn’; ἀντίον ηὔδα is ‘spoke face to face’, ηὔδα being the imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’. πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’ is Telemachus’ stock epithet and is translated every time, even where he is a young man out of his depth. He is about to answer the two questions that Odysseus put to him at the end of the last part.

sentences.t: τοιγὰρ ἐγώ τοι, ξεῖνε, μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως ἀγορεύσω.
sentences.l: “Well then, I will tell you, stranger, very exactly.
sentences.i: “Then I will tell you, stranger, quite exactly.
sentences.n: τοιγάρ ‘well then, therefore’ takes up the questions just asked. ἀγορεύσω is the short-vowel aorist subjunctive of ἀγορεύω ‘tell, speak out’, which Homer can use where Attic would use a future: ‘I will tell’. ἀτρεκέως ‘exactly’ is an adverb in -έως. ξεῖνε is the vocative of ξεῖνος ‘stranger’.

sentences.t:
οὔτε τί μοι πᾶς δῆμος ἀπεχθόμενος χαλεπαίνει,
οὔτε κασιγνήτοις ἐπιμέμφομαι, οἷσί περ ἀνὴρ
μαρναμένοισι πέποιθε, καὶ εἰ μέγα νεῖκος ὄρηται.
sentences.l:
Neither does the whole land, being hateful, harshly rage at me at all,
nor do I blame my brothers, in whom a man
trusts when they fight, even if a great quarrel arises.
sentences.i: Neither is the whole land hostile to me and angry with me, nor do I find fault with my brothers, on whom a man relies when they are fighting, even if a great quarrel has arisen.
sentences.n: These lines answer Odysseus’ two questions in his own words: from οἷσί περ onward they repeat what he asked at the end of the last part, with ἐπιμέμφομαι ‘I find fault with’ for his ἐπιμέμφεαι ‘you find fault with’. οὔτε … οὔτε is ‘neither … nor’, and τί is adverbial ‘at all’. δῆμος is the people of a district and the district itself, and is rendered ‘land’. ἀπεχθόμενος is the participle of ἀπέχθομαι ‘be hateful, be hostile’, and χαλεπαίνει ‘is harshly angry’. οἷσι is the dative plural of the relative ‘in whom’, μαρναμένοισι the dative plural participle ‘when they fight’, and ὄρηται the aorist subjunctive middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rise, arise’.

sentences.t: ὧδε γὰρ ἡμετέρην γενεὴν μούνωσε Κρονίων·
sentences.l: For thus our line the son of Cronus made single:
sentences.i: For the son of Cronus has made our family a lone line in this way:
sentences.n: ὧδε ‘in this way’ looks ahead to the lines that follow. Κρονίων is the patronymic ‘son of Cronus’, that is Zeus, standing alone for the god. ἡμετέρην γενεήν is ‘our family, our line’, with Ionic -ην where Attic has -αν. μούνωσε is the aorist of μουνόω ‘make single, leave alone’, without augment.

sentences.t:
μοῦνον Λαέρτην Ἀρκείσιος υἱὸν ἔτικτε,
μοῦνον δ’ αὖτ’ Ὀδυσῆα πατὴρ τέκεν·
sentences.l:
An only one, Laertes, did Arcesius beget as son,
and an only one, in turn, Odysseus did his father beget;
sentences.i: Arcesius had only one son, Laertes, and Laertes in turn had only one, Odysseus;
sentences.n: Two parallel clauses, each opening with μοῦνον ‘only, as an only one’. Ἀρκείσιος is Arcesius, Laertes’ father, and πατήρ in the second clause is Laertes, so the family has had a single son in each generation; the next unit brings the pattern down to Telemachus. ἔτικτε and τέκεν are both ‘begot’, said of the father, and τέκεν has no augment. αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘in turn’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
μοῦνον ἔμ’ ἐν μεγάροισι τεκὼν λίπεν οὐδ’ ἀπόνητο.
sentences.l:
but Odysseus
an only one, me, in the halls having begotten, left, and had no enjoyment of me.
sentences.i: but Odysseus, having begotten me alone in his halls, left, and had no enjoyment of me.
sentences.n: The third generation: μοῦνον ἔμ’ ‘me alone’ completes the series μοῦνον … μοῦνον. τεκών is the aorist participle of τίκτω ‘beget’, and λίπεν the unaugmented aorist of λείπω ‘leave’. ἀπόνητο is an aorist of ἀπονίναμαι ‘have enjoyment or profit of’, which can take a genitive; here it has no object of its own, and ‘of me’ is supplied from the sense. Telemachus says only that his father had no enjoyment of him.

sentences.t: τῷ νῦν δυσμενέες μάλα μυρίοι εἴσ’ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ.
sentences.l: Therefore now ill-disposed men, very numberless, are in the house.
sentences.i: And so there are now countless ill-disposed men in my house.
sentences.n: τῷ ‘therefore’ is an old instrumental of the pronoun used as a connecting word. δυσμενέες is the uncontracted nominative plural of δυσμενής ‘ill-disposed, hostile’ (from δυσ- ‘bad’ and μένος), and μυρίοι ‘numberless’; εἴσ’ is εἰσί with its ι elided. The next unit names the men.

sentences.t:
ὅσσοι γὰρ νήσοισιν ἐπικρατέουσιν ἄριστοι,
Δουλιχίῳ τε Σάμῃ τε καὶ ὑλήεντι Ζακύνθῳ,
ἠδ’ ὅσσοι κραναὴν Ἰθάκην κάτα κοιρανέουσι,
τόσσοι μητέρ’ ἐμὴν μνῶνται, τρύχουσι δὲ οἶκον.
sentences.l:
For as many as hold power over the islands, the best men,
over Dulichium and Same and wooded Zacynthus,
and as many as are lords throughout rocky Ithaca,
so many woo my mother, and wear out the house.
sentences.i: For all the chief men who hold power in the islands, in Dulichium and Same and wooded Zacynthus, and all who are lords throughout rocky Ithaca — every one of them is wooing my mother and wearing out the house.
sentences.n: These four lines are what Telemachus said of the suitors in Book 1 (1.245–248), apart from a final ν on κοιρανέουσι. ὅσσοι … ὅσσοι … τόσσοι is ‘as many as … as many as … so many’: two relative clauses gathered by one correlative. νήσοισιν is the dative plural in -οισι(ν), ἐπικρατέουσιν the uncontracted ‘hold power’, κοιρανέουσι ‘act as lord’ (from κοίρανος ‘ruler’). Ἰθάκην κάτα is κατὰ Ἰθάκην with the preposition after its noun. μνῶνται is ‘woo’ and τρύχουσι ‘wear out’.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ οὔτ’ ἀρνεῖται στυγερὸν γάμον οὔτε τελευτὴν
ποιῆσαι δύναται·
sentences.l:
And she neither refuses the hateful marriage nor an end
is able to make;
sentences.i: and she neither refuses the marriage she hates nor can bring the matter to an end;
sentences.n: ἡ ‘she’ is a pronoun and means Telemachus’ mother. οὔτε … οὔτε again: ἀρνεῖται ‘refuses’ governs γάμον ‘marriage’, and τελευτήν ‘an end, completion’ is the object of ποιῆσαι δύναται ‘is able to make’. στυγερόν is ‘hateful’. The unit ends at the ano teleia, in the middle of line 127.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δὲ φθινύθουσιν ἔδοντες
οἶκον ἐμόν· τάχα δή με διαρραίσουσι καὶ αὐτόν.
sentences.l:
and they waste away, by eating,
my house; soon indeed they will shatter me, myself as well.
sentences.i: and meanwhile they are eating up my house and wasting it away; and before long they will be the ruin of me too.
sentences.n: τοί ‘they’ is the suitors, the pronoun use of the article. φθινύθουσιν ‘waste, use up’ and ἔδοντες ‘eating’ (present participle of ἔδω) share the object οἶκον ἐμόν ‘my house’. Here the verb is transitive; in line 145 it is intransitive, and the old man’s skin ‘wastes away’. τάχα δή ‘soon indeed’. διαρραίσουσι is the future of διαρραίω ‘break in pieces, ruin utterly’. με … καὶ αὐτόν ‘me, myself as well’ moves the threat from the house to Telemachus himself. The unit ends in the middle of line 128 at the full stop.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι μὲν ταῦτα θεῶν ἐν γούνασι κεῖται·
sentences.l: But truly these things lie on the knees of the gods;
sentences.i: But all this lies on the knees of the gods;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι μέν ‘but truly’ turns from complaint to resignation. θεῶν ἐν γούνασι κεῖται ‘lies on the knees of the gods’ is a formula for what only the gods decide; γούνασι is the dative plural of γόνυ ‘knee’ (Attic γόνασι). The neuter plural ταῦτα ‘these things’ takes a singular verb, κεῖται.

sentences.t:
ἄττα, σὺ δ’ ἔρχεο θᾶσσον, ἐχέφρονι Πηνελοπείῃ
εἴφ’ ὅτι οἱ σῶς εἰμὶ καὶ ἐκ Πύλου εἰλήλουθα.
sentences.l:
Father, but you go more quickly, to sound-minded Penelope
say that safe I am, and from Pylos have come.
sentences.i: Father, now you go quickly, and tell sound-minded Penelope that I am safe and have come from Pylos.
sentences.n: ἄττα is a respectful address by a younger man to an older, ‘father’, with no claim of kinship; Telemachus uses it to Eumaeus. ἔρχεο is the imperative of ἔρχομαι, and θᾶσσον, the comparative of ταχύς, serves in exhortations as ‘quickly’. ἐχέφρονι Πηνελοπείῃ is a dative, ‘sound-minded Penelope’, her stock epithet. εἴφ’ is εἰπέ with π turned to φ before the rough breathing of ὅτι; οἱ ‘to her’ is the enclitic pronoun. σῶς ‘safe’ is the nominative of the adjective, and εἰλήλουθα the perfect of ἔρχομαι.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν αὐτοῦ μενέω, σὺ δὲ δεῦρο νέεσθαι,
οἴῃ ἀπαγγείλας·
sentences.l:
but I here will stay, and you here to come back,
to her alone having reported;
sentences.i: I myself shall stay right here, and you are to come back here once you have told it to her alone;
sentences.n: αὐτοῦ ‘right here’ is an adverb from αὐτός, and μενέω the uncontracted future of μένω ‘remain’. νέεσθαι is an infinitive used as a command, ‘you are to come back’. οἴῃ is the feminine dative of οἶος ‘alone’, ‘to her alone’, looking back to Penelope; ἀπαγγείλας is the aorist participle ‘having reported’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 133.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ἄλλων μή τις Ἀχαιῶν
πευθέσθω·
sentences.l:
and of the others let no one of the Achaeans
learn;
sentences.i: and let none of the other Achaeans find it out;
sentences.n: τῶν δ’ ἄλλων … Ἀχαιῶν is ‘of the other Achaeans’; Ἀχαιοί is a general name for the Greeks, and here means everyone outside the secret. μή τις … πευθέσθω ‘let no one find out’: πευθέσθω is the aorist imperative middle of πεύθομαι ‘learn’.

sentences.t: πολλοὶ γὰρ ἐμοὶ κακὰ μηχανόωνται.
sentences.l: for many against me evils devise.”
sentences.i: for many are devising evils against me.”
sentences.n: πολλοί ‘many’ stands first, for emphasis, and κακά ‘evils’ is the object. μηχανόωνται is the uncontracted present of μηχανάομαι ‘devise’ (Attic μηχανῶνται). The unit closes Telemachus’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφης, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα·
sentences.l: Him, answering, you addressed, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.i: In answer you said to him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.n: A reply formula in the second person: the poet turns from telling about Eumaeus to speaking to him, so προσέφης is ‘you addressed’ and the name stands in the vocative. ἀπαμειβόμενος is ‘answering’ and τόν ‘him’ is Telemachus. συβῶτα is the vocative of συβώτης ‘swineherd’.

sentences.t: γιγνώσκω, φρονέω·
sentences.l: “I know it, I understand;
sentences.i: “I see, I understand;
sentences.n: Eumaeus assents to the order he has just been given. γιγνώσκω ‘I recognise, I know’ and φρονέω ‘I understand, I am aware’ are two verbs for one idea, a quick ‘I have it’.

sentences.t: τά γε δὴ νοέοντι κελεύεις.
sentences.l: these things, indeed, to one who perceives you bid.
sentences.i: you are giving these instructions to a man who understands.
sentences.n: τά γε ‘these things’ is the object of κελεύεις ‘you bid’. νοέοντι is the dative singular masculine participle of νοέω ‘perceive, understand’, ‘to one who understands’: Eumaeus says that he needs no more telling.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον,
sentences.l: But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly;
sentences.i: But come now, tell me this, and set it out for me exactly:
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον is a formula for asking. ἄγε is the imperative ‘come’, used as an exhortation; εἰπέ and κατάλεξον are aorist imperatives, κατάλεξον ‘set out in order, recount’. The unit ends at a comma, because the sentence runs to line 141 and would otherwise be five lines long; the question itself comes in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἦ καὶ Λαέρτῃ αὐτὴν ὁδὸν ἄγγελος ἔλθω
δυσμόρῳ, ὃς τῆος μὲν Ὀδυσσῆος μέγ’ ἀχεύων
ἔργα τ’ ἐποπτεύεσκε μετὰ δμώων τ’ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ
πῖνε καὶ ἦσθ’, ὅτε θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἀνώγοι·
sentences.l:
Am I also to Laertes, on that same road, as messenger to go,
to the ill-fated one, who until then, greatly grieving for Odysseus,
used to oversee the works and, among the servants in the house,
drink and sit, whenever his heart in his breast bade him;
sentences.i: Am I to go on the same journey as a messenger to Laertes too, that ill-fated man, who until then, grieving greatly for Odysseus, used to oversee the work and would drink and sit among the servants in the house whenever his heart in his breast bade him;
sentences.n: ἦ καί opens a question, ‘am I also to …?’, and ἔλθω is the aorist subjunctive of a deliberative question. Murray prints no question mark: the question runs to the end of line 145, and the units follow his stops. δυσμόρῳ ‘ill-fated’ is a dative agreeing with Λαέρτῃ. τῆος ‘until then, for so long’ is answered by νῦν in line 142. ἐποπτεύεσκε has the iterative ending -εσκε ‘used to oversee’, and ἦσθ’ is ἦστο, the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’. ὅτε … ἀνώγοι is an optative with iterative force, ‘whenever his heart bade him’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ νῦν, ἐξ οὗ σύ γε ᾤχεο νηῒ Πύλονδε,
οὔ πω μίν φασιν φαγέμεν καὶ πιέμεν αὔτως,
οὐδ’ ἐπὶ ἔργα ἰδεῖν, ἀλλὰ στοναχῇ τε γόῳ τε
ἧσται ὀδυρόμενος, φθινύθει δ’ ἀμφ’ ὀστεόφι χρώς.
sentences.l:
but now, from the time when you went off in a ship to Pylos,
not yet him, they say, to eat and to drink just so,
nor to look over the works, but with groaning and with lament
he sits mourning, and wastes away about his bones the skin.”
sentences.i: but now, ever since you went off to Pylos in your ship, they say he has not yet eaten or drunk as he used to, nor looked over the work, but sits groaning and lamenting, and his skin is wasting away on his bones?”
sentences.n: ἐξ οὗ ‘from the time when’. νηΐ is the dative of νηῦς, and -δε in Πύλονδε marks motion towards. ᾤχεο is the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘go off’. φαγέμεν and πιέμεν are infinitives in -έμεν (Attic φαγεῖν, πιεῖν). αὔτως is ‘just so’; its sense here, ‘as he used to’, is taken from the contrast with lines 139–141. ἐπὶ … ἰδεῖν is tmesis for ἐφιδεῖν ‘look over’, the same act as ἐποπτεύεσκε in line 140, now left undone. ἧσται is the present of ἧμαι ‘sit’, a verb with perfect-middle endings; ὀστεόφι has the ending -φι; φθινύθει ‘wastes away’ is intransitive. The question, and Eumaeus’ speech, end here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: The same reply formula as at line 112: τόν ‘him’ is Eumaeus this time, αὖ ‘in turn’, and πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’ is Telemachus’ epithet again. It follows a paragraph break in Murray’s text.

sentences.t: ἄλγιον, ἀλλ’ ἔμπης μιν ἐάσομεν, ἀχνύμενοί περ·
sentences.l: “More painful; but all the same we shall let him be, grieving though we are;
sentences.i: “That is more painful, but we shall leave him be all the same, grieving though we are;
sentences.n: ἄλγιον is a comparative, ‘more painful’, with ‘it is’ understood. ἔμπης ‘all the same’. ἐάσομεν is the future of ἐάω ‘let be, leave alone’, and μιν ‘him’ is Laertes. ἀχνύμενοί περ ‘grieving though we are’: περ gives the participle a concessive force.

sentences.t:
εἰ γάρ πως εἴη αὐτάγρετα πάντα βροτοῖσι,
πρῶτόν κεν τοῦ πατρὸς ἑλοίμεθα νόστιμον ἦμαρ.
sentences.l:
for if somehow all things were self-chosen for mortals,
first, of my father, we would choose the homecoming day.
sentences.i: For if everything lay in mortals’ own choosing, the first thing we would choose would be the day of my father’s homecoming.
sentences.n: This gives the reason for the grief: the wish cannot be had. εἰ γάρ πως εἴη ‘for if somehow it were’ is an optative supposition, and κεν … ἑλοίμεθα ‘we would choose’ its answer, an aorist optative middle of αἱρέω ‘take, choose’. αὐτάγρετα, from αὐτός and ἀγρέω ‘take’ (the Aeolic form of αἱρέω), is ‘chosen by oneself’, that is at one’s own option; it is a rare word. νόστιμον ἦμαρ is the ‘homecoming day’ of the proem’s ἀφείλετο νόστιμον ἦμαρ.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σύ γ’ ἀγγείλας ὀπίσω κίε, μηδὲ κατ’ ἀγροὺς
πλάζεσθαι μετ’ ἐκεῖνον·
sentences.l:
But you, having reported, go back, and not through the fields
to wander after him;
sentences.i: But once you have given the message, go back, and do not wander through the fields after him;
sentences.n: ἀγγείλας is the aorist participle of ἀγγέλλω ‘report’, and κίε the imperative of κίω ‘go’; ὀπίσω is ‘back’. μηδὲ … πλάζεσθαι is an infinitive used as a prohibition, ‘and do not wander’; πλάζομαι is ‘wander, be driven astray’. κατ’ ἀγροὺς ‘through the fields’, μετ’ ἐκεῖνον ‘after him’, in pursuit of Laertes.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ πρὸς μητέρα εἰπεῖν
ἀμφίπολον ταμίην ὀτρυνέμεν ὅττι τάχιστα
κρύβδην·
sentences.i: and tell my mother to send out the attendant, the housekeeper, as quickly as possible, and in secret;
sentences.n: εἰπεῖν is an infinitive used as a command, and ὀτρυνέμεν the infinitive of what she is to be told: ‘tell my mother to send’. ὀτρυνέμεν is the infinitive in -έμεν of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on, send quickly’, and its object is ἀμφίπολον ταμίην ‘the attendant, the housekeeper’, a servant of the house. ὅττι τάχιστα ‘as quickly as possible’. κρύβδην ‘secretly’ is an adverb.

sentences.t: κείνη γάρ κεν ἀπαγγείλειε γέροντι.
sentences.l: for she could report it to the old man.”
sentences.i: for she could take word of it to the old man.”
sentences.n: κείνη is the Ionic form of ἐκείνη ‘she’, the housekeeper. ἀπαγγείλειε is the aorist optative of ἀπαγγέλλω, with κεν ‘she could report’. γέροντι ‘the old man’ names Laertes by the one word. The unit closes Telemachus’ speech.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥα καὶ ὦρσε συφορβόν·
sentences.l: He spoke, and roused the swineherd;
sentences.i: So he said, and set the swineherd in motion;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καί ‘he spoke, and’ closes a speech in the narrator’s voice. ῥα is a weak particle ‘so, then’. ὦρσε is the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse, set in motion’. συφορβός ‘swineherd’ (from σῦς ‘swine’ and φέρβω ‘feed’) is the same man as Εὔμαιος ὑφορβός two lines later.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ εἵλετο χερσὶ πέδιλα,
δησάμενος δ’ ὑπὸ ποσσὶ πόλινδ’ ἴεν.
sentences.l:
and he took the sandals in his hands,
and, having bound them under his feet, to the town went.
sentences.i: and he took his sandals in his hands and, binding them on under his feet, set off for the town.
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ ‘and he’ is Eumaeus, with ὁ as a pronoun. πέδιλα are ‘sandals’. δησάμενος is the aorist middle participle of δέω ‘bind’, ‘having bound on’. ποσσί is the dative plural of πούς ‘foot’ (Attic ποσί), πόλινδε is ‘to the town’ with the suffix -δε, and ἴεν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘was going’. The unit ends at a full stop in the middle of line 155.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ Ἀθήνην
λῆθεν ἀπὸ σταθμοῖο κιὼν Εὔμαιος ὑφορβός,
ἀλλ’ ἥ γε σχεδὸν ἦλθε·
sentences.i: And Eumaeus the swineherd, as he left the steading, did not escape Athena’s notice, but she came close;
sentences.n: The grammar is held back until the end of the clause. λῆθεν is the unaugmented aorist of λανθάνω ‘escape the notice of’ and takes the accusative Ἀθήνην ‘Athena’; its subject, Εὔμαιος ὑφορβός, comes last. σταθμοῖο is the genitive in -οιο of σταθμός ‘steading’, and κιών the participle of κίω ‘go’. ἀλλ’ ἥ γε σχεδὸν ἦλθε: ἥ γε is ‘she’, and Athena has seen him go.

sentences.t:
δέμας δ’ ἤϊκτο γυναικὶ
καλῇ τε μεγάλῃ τε καὶ ἀγλαὰ ἔργα ἰδυίῃ.
sentences.l:
and in body she was likened to a woman,
fair and tall and knowing splendid works;
sentences.i: and she took the likeness of a woman, fair and tall and skilled in splendid handiwork;
sentences.n: ἤϊκτο is the pluperfect of ἔοικα ‘be like’, here ‘she was likened’, and takes the dative γυναικί ‘to a woman’. δέμας ‘in body’ is an accusative of respect. ἰδυίῃ is the feminine dative perfect participle of οἶδα ‘know’, agreeing with γυναικί, and ἀγλαὰ ἔργα ἰδυίῃ ‘knowing splendid works’ means skilled in fine handiwork.

sentences.t: στῆ δὲ κατ’ ἀντίθυρον κλισίης Ὀδυσῆϊ φανεῖσα·
sentences.l: and she stood over against the door of the hut, appearing to Odysseus;
sentences.i: and she stood facing the door of the hut, showing herself to Odysseus;
sentences.n: στῆ is the unaugmented aorist of ἵστημι ‘stood’. κατ’ ἀντίθυρον is ‘over against the door’, with κλισίης ‘of the hut’ in the genitive. φανεῖσα is the aorist passive participle of φαίνω, ‘having appeared’, with the dative Ὀδυσῆϊ ‘to Odysseus’. Ὀδυσῆϊ has a single σ: the name has a long and a short form, used as the verse needs them.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα Τηλέμαχος ἴδεν ἀντίον οὐδ’ ἐνόησεν,
οὐ γάρ πω πάντεσσι θεοὶ φαίνονται ἐναργεῖς,
ἀλλ’ Ὀδυσεύς τε κύνες τε ἴδον, καί ῥ’ οὐχ ὑλάοντο
κνυζηθμῷ δ’ ἑτέρωσε διὰ σταθμοῖο φόβηθεν.
sentences.l:
and Telemachus did not see her face to face, nor notice her,
for not yet to all do the gods appear manifest,
but Odysseus and the dogs saw her, and they did not bark,
but with a whine to the other side, through the steading, fled in fear.
sentences.i: And Telemachus did not see her there in front of him, or notice her, for the gods do not appear in manifest form to everyone; but Odysseus saw her, and so did the dogs, and they did not bark, but ran whimpering away through the steading to the far side.
sentences.n: Only Odysseus and the dogs see Athena. ἴδεν and ἐνόησεν are ‘saw’ and ‘noticed’, ἴδεν unaugmented; ἀντίον is the adverb ‘face to face, in front’. οὐ γάρ πω is ‘for not yet’; in a general statement like this the πω adds little, which is why i leaves out ‘yet’. φαίνονται ἐναργεῖς is ‘appear manifest’, ‘in manifest form’ in i. ὑλάοντο is the uncontracted imperfect of ὑλάω ‘bark’, with a middle ending; κνυζηθμῷ is a dative, ‘with a whine’; ἑτέρωσε ‘to the other side’; φόβηθεν is the unaugmented aorist passive of φοβέω, ‘were scared off’.

sentences.t: ἡ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι νεῦσε·
sentences.l: and she, then, with her brows nodded;
sentences.i: and she made a sign with her brows;
sentences.n: ἡ δ’ ἄρ’ ‘and she’ is Athena. νεῦσε is the aorist of νεύω ‘nod, make a sign’, and ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι ‘with her brows’ gives the means; ὀφρύσι is the dative plural of ὀφρύς ‘brow’. The sign is made for Odysseus alone.

sentences.t:
νόησε δὲ δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
ἐκ δ’ ἦλθεν μεγάροιο παρὲκ μέγα τειχίον αὐλῆς,
στῆ δὲ πάροιθ’ αὐτῆς·
sentences.i: and heavenly Odysseus understood, and went out of the hall, past the great wall of the yard, and stood before her;
sentences.n: νόησε is the aorist of νοέω ‘perceive, take her meaning’, and δῖος ‘heavenly’ is Odysseus’ stock epithet. ἐκ δ’ ἦλθεν is ἐξῆλθεν with its preverb set apart (tmesis); μεγάροιο is a genitive in -οιο, ‘out of the hall’, here the main room of the hut. παρέκ ‘out past’ takes the accusative τειχίον, the wall of the yard, with αὐλῆς ‘of the yard’. πάροιθ’ αὐτῆς is ‘before her’. The unit ends at an ano teleia in the middle of line 166.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ προσέειπεν Ἀθήνη·
sentences.l: And him addressed Athena:
sentences.i: And Athena spoke to him:
sentences.n: An approach-and-address formula. τόν ‘him’ is Odysseus. No one has just spoken to Athena, so there is no ‘answered’ and no ‘in turn’; προσέειπεν is ‘addressed’. The name Ἀθήνη comes last.

sentences.t: διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη, πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ.
sentences.l: “Zeus-sprung son of Laertes, many-devising Odysseus.
sentences.i: “Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices.
sentences.n: Athena’s only speech in this part begins with a vocative address. διογενές ‘Zeus-born’ comes from Διός and the root of γένος; Λαερτιάδη is a patronymic, ‘son of Laertes’; πολυμήχαν’ is πολυμήχανε with its last vowel elided, ‘of many devices’; Ὀδυσσεῦ is the vocative of Ὀδυσσεύς. Murray puts a full stop after the vocative, and the unit follows him.

sentences.t:
ἤδη νῦν σῷ παιδὶ ἔπος φάο μηδ’ ἐπίκευθε,
ὡς ἂν μνηστῆρσιν θάνατον καὶ κῆρ’ ἀραρόντε
ἔρχησθον προτὶ ἄστυ περικλυτόν·
sentences.i: Now at last, tell your son the word, and do not keep it hidden, so that the two of you, having prepared death and the spirit of death for the suitors, may go to the very famous town;
sentences.n: φάο is an imperative of φημί ‘say’, and μηδ’ ἐπίκευθε the imperative of ἐπικεύθω ‘conceal’; ἔπος ‘word’ here is what is to be said. ὡς ἄν with the subjunctive means ‘so that’: ἔρχησθον is the dual subjunctive of ἔρχομαι, ‘the two of you may go’, the dual being Odysseus and Telemachus. ἀραρόντε is also dual, the aorist participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit together, make ready’, with the dative μνηστῆρσιν ‘for the suitors’ and the accusatives θάνατον ‘death’ and κῆρα, the death-fate that carries death off. προτί is πρός, and ἄστυ περικλυτόν ‘the very famous town’. The unit ends at an ano teleia in the middle of line 170.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἐγὼ αὐτὴ
δηρὸν ἀπὸ σφῶϊν ἔσομαι μεμαυῖα μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
and not I myself
for long from you two shall be away, eager to fight.”
sentences.i: and I myself shall not be away from the two of you for long, eager as I am to fight.”
sentences.n: σφῶϊν is the dual ‘from you two’. ἔσομαι is ‘I shall be’, with μεμαυῖα, the feminine perfect participle of μέμονα ‘be eager’, and the infinitive μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’. δηρόν is ‘for long’. Athena closes by promising to be at their side; the unit closes her speech.

sentences.t: ἦ καὶ χρυσείῃ ῥάβδῳ ἐπεμάσσατ’ Ἀθήνη.
sentences.l: She spoke, and with a golden wand touched (him), Athena.
sentences.i: So she said, and Athena touched him with a golden wand.
sentences.n: ἦ καί ‘she spoke, and’ closes the speech and opens the action. ἐπεμάσσατ’ is the aorist middle of ἐπιμάσσομαι ‘touch’; its object is not expressed and Odysseus has to be understood. ῥάβδῳ ‘with a wand’ is a dative of means, and χρυσείῃ is the Ionic form of χρυσῇ ‘golden’.

sentences.t:
φᾶρος μέν οἱ πρῶτον ἐϋπλυνὲς ἠδὲ χιτῶνα
θῆκ’ ἀμφὶ στήθεσσι, δέμας δ’ ὤφελλε καὶ ἥβην.
sentences.l:
A cloak first for him, well-washed, and a tunic
she put about his chest, and his body she increased, and his youth.
sentences.i: First she put a well-washed cloak and a tunic about his chest, and increased his stature and his youthful vigour.
sentences.n: φᾶρος is a cloak or mantle, ἐϋπλυνές ‘well-washed’, and οἱ ‘on him’ is the enclitic dative; χιτών is the tunic worn beneath. θῆκ’ is the unaugmented aorist θῆκε ‘put’, with ἀμφὶ στήθεσσι ‘about his chest’, a dative plural in -εσσι. ὤφελλε is the imperfect of ὀφέλλω ‘increase’; δέμας is ‘body, stature’ and ἥβη ‘youth, youthful vigour’.

sentences.t:
ἂψ δὲ μελαγχροιὴς γένετο, γναθμοὶ δὲ τάνυσθεν,
κυάνεαι δ’ ἐγένοντο γενειάδες ἀμφὶ γένειον.
sentences.l:
Back again dark-skinned he became, and his jaws were drawn taut,
and dark grew the beard-hairs about his chin.
sentences.i: His skin turned dark again, his jaws grew taut, and the hair of his beard turned dark around his chin.
sentences.n: μελαγχροιής ‘dark-skinned’ is from μέλας ‘dark’ and χροιά ‘skin, colour’, and ἂψ is ‘back again’. γναθμοί are ‘jaws’, and τάνυσθεν is the unaugmented aorist passive of τανύω ‘stretch, draw taut’. κυάνεαι is ‘dark’, said of the hair; γενειάδες are the hairs of the beard, and ἀμφὶ γένειον ‘around the chin’. Together the lines make the old beggar a man in his prime.

sentences.t: ἡ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς ἔρξασα πάλιν κίεν·
sentences.l: She, then, having so done, went back;
sentences.i: When she had done this, she went away again;
sentences.n: ἡ μέν ‘she’ is answered by αὐτάρ ‘but’ in the next unit. ὣς ἔρξασα ‘having so done’ is the aorist participle of ῥέζω ‘do’, and κίεν the imperfect of κίω ‘go’, πάλιν ‘back’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἤϊεν ἐς κλισίην·
sentences.l:
but Odysseus
went into the hut;
sentences.i: and Odysseus went into the hut;
sentences.n: ἤϊεν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘went’, and ἐς κλισίην ‘into the hut’ is an accusative of goal. Odysseus has been standing before Athena outside, and goes back in as the young man she has made.

sentences.t:
θάμβησε δέ μιν φίλος υἱός,
ταρβήσας δ’ ἑτέρωσε βάλ’ ὄμματα, μὴ θεὸς εἴη,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
and amazed at him was his dear son,
and, frightened, to the other side he cast his eyes, lest it be a god,
and, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: and his dear son was amazed at him, and, afraid that it might be a god, turned his eyes away, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: θάμβησε is the aorist of θαμβέω ‘be amazed’, with μιν ‘at him’. ταρβήσας ‘frightened’ is the aorist participle of ταρβέω; ἑτέρωσε βάλ’ ὄμματα ‘cast his eyes to the other side’ is ‘looked away’. μὴ θεὸς εἴη is a fear clause with the optative: ‘lest it be a god’. καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is a formula: φωνήσας ‘having lifted his voice’, and ‘winged words’ is translated the same way every time.

sentences.t:
ἀλλοῖός μοι, ξεῖνε, φάνης νέον ἠὲ πάροιθεν,
ἄλλα δὲ εἵματ’ ἔχεις, καί τοι χρὼς οὐκέθ’ ὁμοῖος.
sentences.l:
“Different to me, stranger, you appeared just now than before,
and other clothes you have, and your skin is no longer the same.
sentences.i: “Stranger, you appeared different to me just now from the way you were before; you have other clothes, and your skin is no longer the same.
sentences.n: Telemachus names what has changed. ἀλλοῖος ‘different’ goes with φάνης ‘you appeared’, the aorist passive of φαίνω without augment. νέον is here the adverb ‘just now’, not the adjective ‘young’, and ἠέ after the idea of difference means ‘than’. ἄλλα … εἵματα ‘other clothes’; χρώς ‘skin’ is the subject of the last clause, and οὐκέθ’ ὁμοῖος ‘no longer alike’ with it.

sentences.t: ἦ μάλα τις θεός ἐσσι, τοὶ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν·
sentences.l: Truly you are some god, of those who hold the wide heaven;
sentences.i: Surely you are some god, one of those who hold the wide heaven;
sentences.n: ἦ μάλα ‘truly, surely’; ἐσσι is the epic ‘you are’. τοί is here the relative ‘who’, one of the pronoun uses of the article. οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν ‘hold the wide heaven’ is a formula for the gods as the dwellers in heaven; it comes three times in this part, and ‘heaven’ is kept in both layers because it names where they live.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἵληθ’, ἵνα τοι κεχαρισμένα δώομεν ἱρὰ
ἠδὲ χρύσεα δῶρα, τετυγμένα· φείδεο δ’ ἡμέων
sentences.l:
but be gracious, so that pleasing sacrifices we may give you
and golden gifts, wrought; and spare us.”
sentences.i: But be gracious, so that we may give you acceptable sacrifices and well-wrought golden gifts; and spare us.”
sentences.n: ἵληθ’ is ἵληθι ‘be gracious’, an imperative related to ἱλάσκομαι ‘propitiate’. ἵνα with the subjunctive gives the purpose: δώομεν is the Homeric subjunctive of δίδωμι ‘we may give’ (Attic δῶμεν). κεχαρισμένα is the perfect passive participle of χαρίζομαι, ‘pleasing, acceptable’, agreeing with ἱρά, the contracted form of ἱερά ‘sacrifices’. χρύσεα is uncontracted ‘golden’, and τετυγμένα the perfect passive participle of τεύχω, ‘wrought’. φείδεο is the imperative of φείδομαι ‘spare’, with the genitive ἡμέων ‘us’. Murray prints no stop after ἡμέων; the speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him then answered much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus answered him:
sentences.n: A reply formula: τόν ‘him’, ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα ‘answered then’. πολύτλας ‘much-enduring’ (πολύ and the root of τλῆναι ‘endure’) and δῖος ‘heavenly’ are Odysseus’ stock epithets, translated every time.

sentences.t: οὔ τίς τοι θεός εἰμι·
sentences.l: “Not any god to you am I;
sentences.i: “I am no god;
sentences.n: οὔ τίς τοι θεός εἰμι ‘I am no god’: οὔ τις ‘not any’ negates θεός, and τοι is ‘to you, I tell you’. It is the shortest possible answer to Telemachus’ guess.

sentences.t: τί μ’ ἀθανάτοισιν ἐΐσκεις;
sentences.l: why to the immortals do you liken me?
sentences.i: why do you liken me to the immortals?
sentences.n: ἐΐσκεις is the present of ἐΐσκω ‘make like, liken’, with the dative ἀθανάτοισιν ‘to the immortals’; μ’ is με. The question answers the guess he made at line 183.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ πατὴρ τεός εἰμι, τοῦ εἵνεκα σὺ στεναχίζων
πάσχεις ἄλγεα πολλά, βίας ὑποδέγμενος ἀνδρῶν.
sentences.l:
But father yours I am, for whose sake you, groaning,
suffer pains many, the violence of men submitting to.”
sentences.i: No, I am your father, the one for whose sake you groan and suffer many pains, submitting to the violence of men.”
sentences.n: τεός is the epic ‘your’ (Attic σός), and τοῦ εἵνεκα ‘for whose sake’ has the relative use of the article, εἵνεκα being ἕνεκα. στεναχίζων ‘groaning’ and ἄλγεα πάσχεις ‘you suffer pains’ go together. ὑποδέγμενος is a short aorist participle of ὑποδέχομαι, ‘submitting to, taking on’, with the accusative βίας ‘violence’ (the plural of βία) and the genitive ἀνδρῶν ‘of men’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας υἱὸν κύσε, κὰδ δὲ παρειῶν
δάκρυον ἧκε χαμᾶζε·
sentences.l:
So then having spoken, he kissed his son, and down from his cheeks
a tear he let fall to the ground;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and kissed his son, and let a tear fall from his cheeks to the ground;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ‘so then having spoken’ is the narrator’s formula for a speech just made. κύσε is the unaugmented aorist of κυνέω ‘kiss’. κὰδ … ἧκε is tmesis for κατῆκε ‘let fall’, with κὰδ for κατά; παρειῶν ‘from his cheeks’ is a genitive, δάκρυον ‘a tear’, and χαμᾶζε ‘to the ground’ has the suffix -ζε. The unit ends at an ano teleia in the middle of line 191.

sentences.t: πάρος δ’ ἔχε νωλεμὲς αἰεί.
sentences.l: but before, he had held back unceasingly, always.
sentences.i: but until then he had always held back, without a break.
sentences.n: πάρος ‘before, until then’. ἔχε ‘was holding back’ has no object: either his tears or himself has to be understood, and both layers leave it as open as the Greek. νωλεμές ‘without a break’ is an adverb, and αἰεί the epic form of ἀεί ‘always’. Odysseus has held back until now.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχος δ’, οὐ γάρ πω ἐπείθετο ὃν πατέρ’ εἶναι,
ἐξαῦτίς μιν ἔπεσσιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπεν·
sentences.l:
But Telemachus, for not yet was he persuaded that it was his own father,
again, with words, answering him, addressed him:
sentences.i: But Telemachus, who still could not believe that this was his own father, answered him again, and spoke:
sentences.n: ὃν πατέρ’ εἶναι is ‘that he was his own father’: ὅν is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative, and the accusative with the infinitive follows ἐπείθετο ‘was persuaded, believed’. οὐ γάρ πω ‘for not yet’ gives the reason for what he does next. ἐξαῦτις is ‘again’. μιν ἔπεσσιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπεν is ‘answering him with words, addressed him’, the reply formula with the poet’s remark set in the middle of it.

sentences.t:
οὐ σύ γ’ Ὀδυσσεύς ἐσσι, πατὴρ ἐμός, ἀλλά με δαίμων
θέλγει, ὄφρ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον ὀδυρόμενος στεναχίζω.
sentences.l:
“You are not Odysseus, my father, but me some power
enchants, so that still more, lamenting, I may groan.
sentences.i: “You are not Odysseus, my father; some power is enchanting me, so that I may groan and lament still more.
sentences.n: Telemachus does not believe him. ἐσσι is the epic ‘you are’, and σύ γε stresses σύ. δαίμων is a divine power, not a named god. με θέλγει ‘enchants me’ is the present of θέλγω ‘charm, bewitch’. ὄφρα with the subjunctive στεναχίζω ‘so that I may groan’ gives the purpose, and ὀδυρόμενος ‘lamenting’ goes with it.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πως ἂν θνητὸς ἀνὴρ τάδε μηχανόῳτο
ᾧ αὐτοῦ γε νόῳ, ὅτε μὴ θεὸς αὐτὸς ἐπελθὼν
ῥηϊδίως ἐθέλων θείη νέον ἠὲ γέροντα.
sentences.l:
For not at all could a mortal man this devise
by his own mind, unless a god himself, coming upon him,
easily, wishing, could make him young or old.
sentences.i: For no mortal man could devise this by his own mind, unless a god himself came upon him and, if he wished, easily made him young or old.
sentences.n: μηχανόῳτο is the uncontracted optative of μηχανάομαι ‘devise’ (Attic μηχανῷτο), the optative of what could happen. ᾧ αὐτοῦ γε νόῳ is ‘by his own mind’: ᾧ is the possessive ‘his own’ and αὐτοῦ strengthens it. ὅτε μή is ‘unless’. θείη is the aorist optative of τίθημι ‘make’, so θείη νέον ἠὲ γέροντα is ‘could make him young or old’; ἐπελθών ‘coming upon him’. Here νέον is the adjective ‘young’, not the adverb of line 181.

sentences.t: ἦ γάρ τοι νέον ἦσθα γέρων καὶ ἀεικέα ἕσσο·
sentences.l: Truly, for just now you were an old man, and in unseemly (things) you were clothed;
sentences.i: For a moment ago you were an old man, dressed in unseemly clothes;
sentences.n: ἦσθα is the epic ‘you were’. νέον is the adverb ‘just now’, as in line 181. ἕσσο is ‘you were clothed’, a pluperfect passive of ἕννυμι, with ἀεικέα ‘unseemly’ in the neuter plural; ‘clothes’ is understood. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: νῦν δὲ θεοῖσιν ἔοικας, οἳ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσι.
sentences.l: but now you are like the gods, who hold the wide heaven.”
sentences.i: but now you look like the gods who hold the wide heaven.”
sentences.n: θεοῖσιν ἔοικας ‘you are like gods’ takes the dative. οἳ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσι is the formula of line 183 again; he took the stranger for an old beggar a moment ago and says that he looks like a god now.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: A reply formula: ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη ‘answering, addressed’. πολύμητις ‘of many wiles’ (πολύ and μῆτις ‘cunning intelligence’) is another stock epithet of Odysseus, distinct from the πολυμήχανος of line 167.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, οὔ σε ἔοικε φίλον πατέρ ἔνδον ἐόντα
οὔτε τι θαυμάζειν περιώσιον οὔτ’ ἀγάασθαι·
sentences.l:
“Telemachus, it is not fitting that you at your dear father, being within,
either marvel exceedingly or be amazed;
sentences.i: “Telemachus, it is not fitting for you to marvel so greatly at your dear father when he is here at home, or to be amazed at him;
sentences.n: A gentle rebuke. οὔ σε ἔοικε ‘it is not fitting for you’ takes an infinitive. φίλον πατέρ ἔνδον ἐόντα is ‘your dear father being within’, the object of θαυμάζειν ‘marvel at’, with πατέρ for πατέρα (the elision mark is not printed). οὔτε τι … οὔτ’ ‘neither at all … nor’; περιώσιον is ‘beyond measure, exceedingly’. ἀγάασθαι is the uncontracted infinitive of ἀγάομαι ‘be amazed at’.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γάρ τοι ἔτ’ ἄλλος ἐλεύσεται ἐνθάδ’ Ὀδυσσεύς,
ἀλλ’ ὅδ’ ἐγὼ τοιόσδε, παθὼν κακά, πολλὰ δ’ ἀληθείς,
ἤλυθον εἰκοστῷ ἔτεϊ ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν.
sentences.i: No other Odysseus will come here any more; here I am, as you see me, after suffering evils and wandering much, come in the twentieth year to my fatherland.
sentences.n: ἔτ’ ἄλλος ‘any other, any more’. ὅδ’ ἐγὼ τοιόσδε is ‘here I am, such as I am’. παθών is the aorist participle of πάσχω, with κακά ‘evils’. ἀληθείς is the aorist passive participle of ἀλάομαι ‘wander’; it is not the adjective ἀληθής ‘true’. ἤλυθον is the Homeric by-form of ἦλθον, and εἰκοστῷ ἔτεϊ ‘in the twentieth year’ a dative of time, ἔτεϊ being the epic dative of ἔτος ‘year’. πατρίδα γαῖαν ‘fatherland’.

sentences.t:
αὐτάρ τοι τόδε ἔργον Ἀθηναίης ἀγελείης,
ἥ τέ με τοῖον ἔθηκεν, ὅπως ἐθέλει, δύναται γάρ,
ἄλλοτε μὲν πτωχῷ ἐναλίγκιον, ἄλλοτε δ’ αὖτε
ἀνδρὶ νέῳ καὶ καλὰ περὶ χροῒ εἵματ’ ἔχοντι.
sentences.l:
But to you this is the work of Athena the spoil-driver,
who made me such, as she wishes, for she is able,
at one time like to a beggar, at another time again
to a young man, and with fine clothes about his skin.
sentences.i: But this is the work of Athena, the driver of spoil, who has made me what I am, in whatever way she wishes, for she is able: at one time like a beggar, at another like a young man with fine clothes on his body.
sentences.n: Odysseus gives the cause. ἔργον Ἀθηναίης ἀγελείης ‘the work of Athena, the spoil-driver’; the sense of ἀγελείη is not certain, probably from ἄγω ‘drive’ and λεία ‘booty’. ἥ τε: ἥ is the relative ‘who’, and τε gives it a general colour. τοῖον ‘such (as you see)’; ὅπως ἐθέλει ‘as she wishes’; δύναται γάρ ‘for she can’. ἄλλοτε μέν … ἄλλοτε δέ is ‘at one time … at another’. ἐναλίγκιον ‘like to’ agrees with με and takes the datives πτωχῷ ‘a beggar’ and ἀνδρὶ νέῳ ‘a young man’; ἔχοντι ‘having’ agrees with ἀνδρί, and χροΐ is the dative of χρώς ‘skin’.

sentences.t:
ῥηΐδιον δὲ θεοῖσι, τοὶ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν,
ἠμὲν κυδῆναι θνητὸν βροτὸν ἠδὲ κακῶσαι.
sentences.l:
And easy for the gods, who hold the wide heaven,
both to glorify a mortal man and to afflict him.”
sentences.i: And it is easy for the gods who hold the wide heaven both to give glory to a mortal man and to afflict him.”
sentences.n: ῥηΐδιον is ‘easy’, with ἐστί understood, and θεοῖσι ‘for the gods’ is the dative of the persons concerned; ῥηϊδίως in line 198 is the adverb of the same word. τοὶ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν is the formula of lines 183 and 200 for the third time. ἠμὲν … ἠδέ is ‘both … and’. κυδῆναι is an aorist infinitive of κυδαίνω ‘give glory to’ (from κῦδος ‘glory’), and κακῶσαι of κακόω ‘treat badly, afflict’. θνητὸν βροτόν ‘a mortal man’ puts two words for ‘mortal’ together. The unit closes Odysseus’ speech.
